Recognition & Management of Abnormal Pregnancy

Abnormal pregnancy — bleeding in early and late pregnancy, hypertensive disorders, anaemia, diabetes, multiple pregnancy and malpresentation.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Recognise bleeding in early and late pregnancy
  • Diagnose and manage pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
  • Describe management of anaemia, diabetes and multiple pregnancy
  • Identify malpresentation and abnormal liquor

In simple words

High-risk means the pregnancy carries danger to the mother or baby. Most problems can be prevented from becoming emergencies with early detection, specialist care and hospital delivery.

Bleeding in early pregnancy

Condition Features Management
Abortion Bleeding, cramping, expulsion of products Rest, anti-D, emptying the uterus
Ectopic pregnancy Amenorrhoea, unilateral pain, bleeding, dizziness Emergency surgical management
Molar pregnancy Large uterus, high hCG, vomiting, bleeding Evacuation and follow-up of hCG

Bleeding in late pregnancy (APH)

Type Features
Placenta praevia Painless, bright red, recurrent bleeding; placenta covers the cervix; NO vaginal examination
Abruptio placentae Painful, dark blood, tense tender uterus, fetal distress
Others Vasa praevia, local cervical lesions

Management: admit, IV line, cross-match, ultrasound, expectant care or surgical delivery. Never do a vaginal examination before excluding placenta praevia.

Hypertensive disorders

  • Gestational hypertension — BP above 140/90 after 20 weeks without proteinuria
  • Pre-eclampsia — hypertension with proteinuria, oedema, headache and reduced fetal growth
  • Eclampsia — convulsions; airway, magnesium sulfate is first-line, delivery when stable
  • HELLP — haemolysis, raised liver enzymes, low platelets

🔴 Magnesium sulfate for fits

In eclampsia, give magnesium sulfate as ordered — watch for toxicity: absent knee jerk, respiratory depression, urine output under 25 mL per hour; keep calcium gluconate ready as the antidote.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Placenta praevia causes painless, bright red bleeding.
  2. Abruptio placentae causes painful bleeding with a tense, tender uterus.
  3. Never examine the vagina before excluding placenta praevia.
  4. Pre-eclampsia = hypertension plus proteinuria after 20 weeks.
  5. Eclampsia is treated with magnesium sulfate.
  6. High-risk pregnancies need hospital delivery.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. HELLP: haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets.
  2. Magnesium sulfate toxicity causes absent reflexes and slow breathing.
  3. Anaemia below 11 g/dL in pregnancy is a high-risk sign.
  4. Multiple pregnancy carries more risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and preterm birth.
  5. Breech may be turned by external cephalic version before labour.

📌 Memory trick

Bleeding: placenta praevia = painless bright red; abruptio = painful dark blood.

60-second revision

  • Early bleeding: abortion, ectopic, molar.
  • Late bleeding: placenta praevia (painless), abruptio (painful).
  • Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia with magnesium sulfate.
  • Anaemia, diabetes, heart disease need specialist care.
  • Multiple pregnancy and malpresentation need extra monitoring.

Test yourself

Painless, bright red bleeding after 28 weeks suggests:

Answer: B. Painless recurrent bright red bleeding is typical of placenta praevia.

The drug of choice for eclampsia is:

Answer: B. Magnesium sulfate is the first-line drug to prevent and control seizures in eclampsia.

A tense tender uterus with dark blood suggests:

Answer: B. Abruptio placentae causes painful bleeding with a tense tender uterus and fetal distress.

Pre-eclampsia is diagnosed when there is hypertension with:

Answer: B. Pre-eclampsia is hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria, with or without oedema.

A nurse must not do a vaginal examination when:

Answer: B. Vaginal examination can provoke severe bleeding in placenta praevia and is contraindicated.
